title: Measure, then stop allocating
sub: Bytes per call, MemoryDiagnoser, ArrayPool, stackalloc and string.Create
cards/0/body:
Before removing allocations, find out how many there are. The most precise counter at hand is GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(): how many bytes the current thread has allocated over its lifetime. The runtime keeps it in the same allocation context, so the call is cheap and the "after minus before" difference is exact to the object.

Two rules:

  • warm the code up with one call first: the first call pulls in the JIT, static constructors, lazy caches;
  • the counter is per thread: if the work moves to another thread (Task.Run, the thread pool), it will not see it.
cards/0/deep: The counter is the allocation context's alloc_bytes plus alloc_bytes_uoh minus the unused remainder of the current chunk — which is why it is exact even though chunks are handed out 8 KB at a time. .NET Framework got this method only in version 4.8; before that you had to look at AppDomain.MonitoringTotalAllocatedMemorySize or at performance counters.
cards/1/q: The measurement shows 0 bytes, although the profiler sees thousands of objects per call. Why?
cards/1/options/0: The work ran on a pool thread, and the counter only counts the current thread
cards/1/options/1: The counter ignores objects the GC has already collected
cards/1/options/2: Without a warm-up the counter always returns 0
cards/1/explain: ProcessBatch ran on another thread, so its bytes went into that thread's context. This kind of measurement needs GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes — the sum over all threads. The counter is monotonic: collections never decrease it.
cards/1/wrong/1: The counter counts what was allocated, not what is alive: collected objects are not subtracted from it.
cards/2/body:
GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise) (.NET Core 3.0+) is how much the whole process has allocated. With precise: false the result may miss the remainders of the threads' current chunks; true is more exact but noticeably more expensive.

To compare code variants, use BenchmarkDotNet with the [MemoryDiagnoser] attribute. The table gains columns:

  • Allocated — bytes per operation;
  • Gen0, Gen1, Gen2 — how many collections of each generation happened per 1000 operations.

In a running service, watch the allocation rate: the allocation rate counter in dotnet-counters (covered in the unit "How to measure").
cards/3/q: MemoryDiagnoser reports for a method: Allocated = 160 B, Gen0 = 0.0153. What does it mean?
cards/3/options/0: Each call allocates 160 bytes; there are about 0.015 generation 0 collections per 1000 calls
cards/3/options/1: Each call allocates 160 bytes and triggers 0.0153 collections
cards/3/options/2: The method keeps 160 bytes alive, 1.5% of which survive generation 0
cards/3/options/3: The whole run allocated 160 bytes, with almost no collections
cards/3/explain: Allocated is bytes per operation, the GenN columns are collections per 1000 operations. That is one generation 0 collection per roughly 65,000 calls: 160 bytes × 65,000 ≈ 10 MB — the order of a generation 0 budget.
cards/3/wrong/1: The number in the Gen0 column is per 1000 operations, not per one.
cards/4/body:
A temporary buffer does not have to be allocated anew. ArrayPool<T>.Shared is a shared pool of arrays:

  • Rent(n) hands out an array of length at least n — usually the next power of two, so always remember your own length;
  • Return(array) gives it back; by default the contents are not cleared, for secrets there is clearArray: true;
  • after Return the array is no longer yours.

Inside, the pool has a per-thread cache and sets of arrays per core, so Rent and Return almost always avoid locks. For the buffers from the LOH lesson this is the cure: a megabyte is allocated once and lives in generation 2 instead of being created for every request.
cards/4/deep: The shared pool keeps arrays from 16 to 2³⁰ elements long, one bucket per power of two; for a bigger request it allocates a plain array and drops it on return. Under memory pressure the pool trims unused arrays by itself. Failing to return an array is not a leak — the GC collects it, the pool just does not help. A custom pool with other limits is ArrayPool<T>.Create(maxArrayLength, maxArraysPerBucket).
cards/5/q: The checksum sometimes does not match. Which line is wrong?
cards/5/explain: Rent(count) returned an array of at least count elements, usually more. Checksum(buf) also covers the tail, which holds the previous renter's data. It should be Checksum(buf.AsSpan(0, count)).
cards/6/title: stackalloc + Span: small things go on the stack
cards/6/body:
Span<T> and stackalloc themselves are covered in the unit "Performance" of the "Deeper C#" course. Here is a working pattern for memory: a small buffer comes from the stack, a large one from the pool.

Keep the threshold small — usually hundreds of bytes, up to a couple of kilobytes: the thread stack is limited (the stack lesson in the unit "Memory through the OS’s eyes"), and an overflow cannot be caught. Never pass a size taken from input to stackalloc without a check.
cards/6/deep: stackalloc zeroes the buffer: locals in .NET are zero-initialized (the localsinit flag in IL). The [SkipLocalsInit] attribute (C# 9, requires AllowUnsafeBlocks) turns it off for a method or a type — then the buffer holds garbage and must not be read before it is written. The gain shows on buffers of hundreds of bytes in hot methods.
cards/7/q: Complete the "small on the stack, large from the pool" pattern
cards/7/explain: The stackalloc branch does not touch the heap; the pool branch rents an array and must return it. new byte[512] would work, but it would allocate a heap object on every call.
cards/8/title: string.Create: a string without an intermediate buffer
cards/8/body:
If the length of the final string is known up front, you can fill it in place. string.Create(length, state, action) allocates a string of the needed length and hands you its characters as a Span<char>. One allocation — the string itself, no StringBuilder and no temporary char[].

The state is passed as an argument and the lambda is marked static: that way it captures nothing and the compiler caches the delegate.
cards/8/deep: Strings are immutable for everyone who can see them — but inside string.Create nobody has seen the string yet, so writing to it is safe. Do not keep the span beyond the lambda: after it returns, the string becomes an ordinary immutable one. Interpolation $"..." since C# 10 often gives a comparable result with no manual work; string.Create is for when the format is unusual or you need the exact length.
cards/9/body:
The compiler caches a non-capturing lambda by itself. So the task is to get rid of the capture. Good APIs take the state as a separate argument for this: ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd, string.Create, ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem, CancellationToken.Register.

The static keyword before a lambda (C# 9) turns "I hope there is no capture here" into a compiler check. If the delegate does carry state but is always the same, create it once and keep it in a field.
cards/10/q: The code returned an array to the pool and kept reading from it. What happens?
cards/10/options/0: Usually it works, but sometimes it sends someone else's data: the array may already belong to another renter
cards/10/options/1: An ObjectDisposedException when the array is accessed
cards/10/options/2: Nothing bad: Return only marks the array while references to it exist
cards/10/options/3: The GC collects the array and Send reads freed memory
cards/10/explain: The pool does not know you still hold a reference and checks nothing. The next Rent on this or another thread may get the same array and write to it while your Send runs. The bug does not crash, it silently corrupts data — which is why Return goes in finally, after the last use.
cards/10/wrong/3: The array is an ordinary managed object: while a reference to it exists, the GC leaves it alone. The problem is different — shared ownership.
cards/11/q: Match the task and the tool
cards/11/pairs/0/0: A temporary buffer of hundreds of KB
cards/11/pairs/1/0: A 128-byte buffer in a hot method
cards/11/pairs/2/0: A string of known length built from parts
cards/11/pairs/3/0: A GetOrAdd factory in hot code
cards/11/pairs/3/1: A static lambda with state as an argument
